books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, January 1, 1831
Frederick Douglass, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, July 5, 1852

stimulus.source_note: John Brown, note written on the morning of his execution, December 2, 1859. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood. I had, as I now think, vainly flattered myself that without very much bloodshed it might be done.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Garrison’s Liberator, Douglass’s speeches, and Brown’s raid show three abolitionist tactics. The three together best illustrate that abolitionists

options.text: agreed on a single plan for ending slavery.
options.misconception: Background from the books: abolitionists argued over tactics, from moral suasion to politics to violence; the three men show the argument, not an agreement.

options.text: all rejected the use of the written word.
options.misconception: Garrison’s paper and Douglass’s speeches are the written and spoken word at work; only Brown turned to arms.

options.text: disagreed about the means, while sharing one goal.
worked only through the courts and Congress.
options.misconception: Background from the books: none of the three worked mainly through courts or Congress; the press, the platform, and the armory were their chosen ground.

rationales.A: Background from the books: abolitionists argued over tactics, from moral suasion to politics to violence; the three men show the argument, not an agreement.
rationales.B: Garrison’s paper and Douglass’s speeches are the written and spoken word at work; only Brown turned to arms.
rationales.C: Background from the books: one man wrote, one man spoke, one man seized an armory — three different means aimed at one end, the destruction of slavery.
rationales.D: Background from the books: none of the three worked mainly through courts or Congress; the press, the platform, and the armory were their chosen ground.
rationales.general:
1. Name each man’s tool: Garrison the press, Douglass the platform, Brown the rifle.
2. Background from the books: abolitionists debated tactics through the 1850s, some trusting words, a few turning to violence.
3. Hold the two truths together: the means divided them, and the goal united them.
Remember: a movement is often one goal carried by many tactics; sort the tactics before you judge the movement.
